newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian government banks on budget for boost.
newsitem.headline: Australian government banks on budget for boost.

text.p: Australia's conservative government, barely a year old, is banking on its second budget this week to recover the support of voters unhappy with its failure to fix the country's problems immediately.

Tuesday's budget for fiscal 1997/98 starting July 1 is supposed to deliver a surplus within two years. Analysts expect a second round of fiscal cuts, but Prime Minister John Howard promises it will be popular among disgruntled supporters.
"Next week's budget will be very good for jobs, it will be very good for small business and it will be very good for the regions of Australia," he said last week, without elaborating.
Howard's government rode high in the opinion polls after its March 1996 election victory, and its deficit-slashing budget in August attracted the support of more voters.

But its standing in the opinion polls has slumped in the past few weeks. Many voters have fled to the new and controversial One Nation Party of populist MP Pauline Hanson, who opposes Aboriginal welfare, Asian immigration and economic reform.
Howard said the distraction of budget preparation had prevented the government selling its policies lately.
"We're going through a period at the moment where the government is quite understandably preoccupied," he said. "We've been tied down preparing the budget."
The budget is supposed to return public finances to the surplus position last seen before the 1990/91 recession.
Last year's budget implemented big savings, worth A$7 billion (US$5.5 billion), or 1.5 percent of gross domestic product.

After those cuts it was thought the government was within easy reach of its promised 1997/98 surplus, but Treasurer Peter Costello said in January the budget was in worse shape than at first thought. He deferred the surplus target to 1998/99 and said further cuts would be needed to achieve it.
On Costello's January figures, more than A$2 billion in cuts would be needed, but analysts now say the budget has probably improved again.
They expect A$2 billion in cuts, a 1997/98 budget approaching balance and a 1998/99 surplus with cash to spare for tax breaks or other giveaways before the election due in early 1999.
But Costello said on Sunday some analysts forecasting a better than expected budget deficit for the year to June 30, 1998 were being too optimistic.

Costello has flagged a crackdown on tax exemptions as one source of extra revenue, but the pre-budget period has not seen the sort of leaks that often emanate from disgruntled public servants targeted for cuts.
If the budget fails to cut heavily it may be because Howard is concerned about the falling opinion polls.
The government generally led the opposition by 12 to 18 percentage points throughout 1996, but its lead has crashed to about six points in recent weeks as supporters have shifted to Hanson.
Howard says Australians held enormous expectations for his coalition when it ousted the 13-year-old Labor government last year and have been disappointed that everything did not change immediately.
"I know there are some people out there who voted for us in March of last year who would have liked to have seen more change," he said last week.
The Australian economy has performed only moderately well since Howard took office. GDP grew 3.1 percent in 1996, but the unemployment rate has been stuck around 8.5 percent. (A$1 = US$0.78)
